outcome_analysis.explanation: This is serial_only_pass from the completed official evaluations: parallel scored 0/40 and serial scored 40/40. The concrete process difference is delivery state, not difficulty of the Rust port. Parallel produced a byte-exact project in one implementer, but a later implementer retry sharing /output removed the project tree and the parent never recovered before timeout, so artifact validation copied no files. Serial kept one coherent workspace owner, retained the Cargo project and test19.rs, verified byte equality, and those files were copied into evaluation.
parallel_contributors: A later parallel implementer retry cleared the shared final /output tree after another implementer had already produced a byte-exact candidate.
The workflow was killed before repair/final-gate recovery, and artifact validation recorded an empty file list.
serial_contributors: The serial agent wrote and retained a complete Cargo project with root test19.rs and source modules.
The serial agent verified byte equality across multiple argument sets and artifact validation copied the files for official evaluation.
ordinary_implementation_differences: No ordinary algorithmic defect is needed to explain the official gap; the parallel implementation was verified before being removed.
outcome_analysis.causal_scope: supported comparative contributors, not an exclusive root cause

candidates.reason: The workflow explicitly assigned an implement child for the full Rust port, and that child produced files and ran verification before later cleanup.
The implementation was not split into independent incompatible component implementations; a single implementer owned the integrated project.
The implement prompt assigned the root test19.rs, Cargo project, modules, and binaries, and one implementer assembled those artifacts in /output.
The workflow script owned spec, implement, verify, repair, and final-gate stages; the failure is the later shared-tree cleanup, not an unowned pipeline.
The spec phase was deliberate preparation and did not itself block implementation from completing a byte-exact candidate.
Investigation results were produced and used in an implementation prompt; the adverse event occurred after implementation, when a retry cleared the workspace.
The critical implementation path had enough capacity to build a byte-exact tree; the missing delivery came from deletion of that tree.
There was repeated retrying and a timeout, but the concrete adverse boundary was a broad /output cleanup that removed already verified files.
The implement assignment was broad but demonstrably completed once; no single overbroad child scope is the specific cause of the final empty artifact.
The implement brief included the known project layout, byte-equality, no-crate, and root-entry requirements; the retry failed by clearing existing files, not by following a missing requirement.
No independently produced components had an observed interface mismatch; the successful project tree was later removed wholesale.
No known requirement or finding is proven lost in transfer; the retry saw existing content and chose a cleanup command.
The component specs were large, but an implementer used them to create a byte-exact project, so overload did not cause unconsumed work.
There is no evidence that a receiver acted on superseded state; the harmful action was direct deletion of current output files.
No incompatible handoff reports remained unadjudicated at a decision point; the observed mismatch is a filesystem overwrite/deletion.
The parallel parent did not present the whole task as complete; final.txt is empty and the workflow status is killed, while evaluator/status evidence alone cannot establish this label.
The implement retry is part of the same episode, but the actionable and directly evidenced boundary is the retry clearing the final workspace after observing pre-existing files.
